blocks.text: A urine specimen container is a purpose-designed container used to collect, transport and store urine for laboratory testing. It is a simple but important OSCE station because specimen quality directly affects diagnostic accuracy.
You should be able to identify the container, select the correct type, explain specimen collection, prevent contamination, recognise unsuitable samples and describe safe handling.
Name: Urine specimen container or urine collection pot.
Classification: Specimen collection and transport equipment.

items.text: Usually made of transparent or translucent plastic.
Has a wide opening for convenient collection.
Usually has a screw-cap lid to prevent leakage.
May have graduations to estimate urine volume.
Usually has a label area for patient identification.
Some types are sterile; others are intended for non-sterile collection or specific uses.

blocks.text: A. Sterile urine specimen container
Used when microbiological testing, such as urine culture, is required. It should remain sterile internally until collection.
B. Routine urine collection container
Used for selected routine urinalysis tests when accepted by the laboratory. It is not automatically suitable for culture.
C. Twenty-four-hour urine collection container
A larger container used to collect all urine passed during a specified 24-hour period for quantitative investigations.
D. Pediatric urine collection bag
An adhesive collection device used in infants and young children. It can be useful for screening, but contamination makes it unsuitable for reliably confirming a positive urine culture.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is a urine specimen container used to collect and transport urine for laboratory analysis. Depending on the investigation, the container may need to be sterile, leak-proof and appropriately labelled.”

blocks.text: Examiner tip: The most important issue is not the appearance of the pot; it is whether the specimen is correctly collected, labelled, stored and transported for the requested test.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to collect a urine specimen — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: “I need to collect a urine specimen for laboratory testing. I will explain how to collect it so that contamination is minimised.”
Confirm identity, explain the test and obtain consent where appropriate.
Use a sterile container for urine culture when required. For a timed collection or specialised test, obtain the specific container and instructions from the laboratory.
Label according to institutional policy, ensuring that the specimen can be linked to the correct patient. Complete the request form with the relevant clinical information.

blocks.title: For a routine clean-catch midstream specimen:

items.text: Wash hands.
Clean the genital area according to the supplied instructions.
Begin passing urine into the toilet.
Without interrupting the stream if possible, collect the midstream portion in the container.
Avoid touching the inside of the container or lid.
Finish passing urine into the toilet.

blocks.text: The exact cleansing instructions may differ by local protocol and patient circumstances.
Replace the lid immediately and tighten it securely. Avoid touching the inside of the lid or container.

items.text: The container is correctly labelled.

The lid is secure.

blocks.text: Do not reject a specimen based on appearance alone; assess suitability according to the requested test and laboratory policy.
Record the collection date and time and any special collection details required by the laboratory.

Send the specimen to the laboratory promptly. If processing is delayed, follow the laboratory's validated storage requirements. Depending on the test, refrigeration or an approved preservative may be needed.

content_groups.group_title: Step 9: Dispose of materials and perform hand hygiene

blocks.text: Discard used cleansing materials and PPE appropriately. Clean any contaminated surfaces according to local policy.
Identify → Select → Label → Collect → Secure → Check → Transport.

For a typical 24-hour collection, the patient empties the bladder at the designated start time and discards that first specimen, records the time, and then collects all subsequent urine, including the final specimen at the same time the following day. The first specimen is discarded because it marks the start of the collection period rather than contributing to it.
The exact procedure may differ by test. Follow the laboratory's instructions regarding refrigeration, preservatives and collection volume. Missing a void can invalidate the collection.
A urine specimen container itself has no meaningful medical contraindication. The main risks arise from poor collection technique, specimen handling and inappropriate container selection.

content_groups.group_title: What if the specimen is contaminated?

blocks.text: Assess the type of test, collection method and degree of contamination. If the specimen is unsuitable, recollect it when clinically appropriate. Do not automatically interpret a contaminated culture as a confirmed infection.
Handle it using the laboratory's biological-spill and specimen-rejection procedures. If necessary, arrange recollection in a suitable leak-proof container.
Unlike a urine dipstick, a specimen container does not itself generate a diagnostic result. However, the specimen's appearance and suitability can provide useful preliminary information.
A. Typical appearance

items.text: Usually clear and pale yellow to amber.
Colour varies with hydration, diet, medications and other factors.
A normal appearance does not exclude urinary disease.

blocks.text: B. Cloudy urine
Possible causes include crystals, cells, mucus, contamination or infection. Cloudiness alone does not diagnose a UTI.
C. Red or pink urine
May result from blood, foods, medications or pigments. Visible haematuria requires appropriate clinical assessment.
D. Dark brown or tea-coloured urine
May occur with concentrated urine, blood pigments, bilirubin or other causes. Further assessment depends on symptoms and investigations.
E. Visible sediment
May represent crystals, cells, mucus or contamination. Microscopy may be required to determine its significance.

blocks.text: OSCE distinction: A specimen may appear normal but still be unsuitable because it is mislabelled, contaminated or improperly stored. Conversely, an abnormal appearance does not establish a diagnosis.
Collecting urine from infants and young children requires an age-appropriate method that minimises contamination and distress.
When feasible, a clean-catch specimen can be collected using an appropriate technique. It is often preferred when a reliable specimen can be obtained without invasive procedures.

items.text: START: Begin urinating into the toilet.
MID: Collect the midstream urine in the container.
STOP: Remove the container, finish urinating and secure the lid.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the purpose of a urine specimen container?
Answer: To collect, contain and transport urine safely for laboratory testing.
Q2. Why is a sterile container used for urine culture?
Answer: It minimises contamination from the container itself, helping produce a more reliable microbiological result. Correct collection technique is still essential.
Q3. What is a midstream urine specimen?
Answer: A specimen collected from the middle portion of the urine stream after the initial urine has been passed into the toilet.
Q4. Why must the specimen be labelled correctly?
Answer: To ensure that the result is assigned to the correct patient and to prevent diagnostic and treatment errors.
Q5. Can a urine collection bag confirm UTI in an infant?

Answer: A positive culture from a bag specimen is prone to contamination and should not ordinarily be used alone to confirm UTI. A reliable specimen should be obtained according to the clinical circumstances and local guideline.
Q6. How is a 24-hour urine specimen collected?

Answer: The patient discards the first urine at the designated start time, collects all urine for the next 24 hours, and includes the final specimen at the same time the following day, following the laboratory's specific instructions.
Q7. What should you do if the container is leaking?
Answer: Follow the laboratory's spill and specimen-rejection procedures, ensure safe containment and arrange recollection if necessary.
Q8. Does cloudy urine mean the patient has a UTI?
Answer: No. Cloudiness can result from cells, crystals, mucus, contamination or infection. Further assessment is needed.
Q9. What is the purpose of a secondary specimen bag?
Answer: It provides secondary containment to reduce leakage exposure and may separate the specimen from its accompanying paperwork.
Q10. What should you check before sending a urine specimen to the laboratory?
Answer: Correct identification, appropriate container, adequate volume, secure closure, collection time and compliance with the laboratory's storage and transport requirements.
Mistake: Touching the inside of the container
This may contaminate the specimen. Keep the inner surfaces clean and avoid placing the lid on a contaminated surface.
Mistake: Using a non-sterile container for a culture when a sterile one is required
Select the container according to the laboratory's requirements.
Mistake: Forgetting the collection date and time
Accurate collection details are important for specimen traceability and timed urine tests.
Mistake: Failing to secure the lid
Tighten the lid and check for leakage before transport.
Mistake: Treating a positive bag culture as definitive in an infant
Remember the high contamination risk and use an appropriate confirmatory collection method.
Examiner tip: Explain why specimen quality matters
The diagnostic value of the laboratory result depends heavily on correct patient identification, collection, storage and transport.
